newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's planned lira bond seen part of strategy.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's planned lira bond seen part of strategy.

text.p: A planned lira bond issue from the Mexican federal government fits in with the government's strategy of going to market early and often this year, analysts said Monday.
With key mid-term elections in July, Mexican borrowers in general are seen taking advantage of what could be the calm before the storm.
Market sources say the federal government, the United Mexican States (UMS), will place a 500 billion lira 10-year Eurobond, perhaps this Wednesday.
The floating-rate note is tipped to be led by Chase Manhattan Bank.
In November last year, the UMS placed a five-year lira issue, worth about $325 million, at 249 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries.
"They need to place more issues this year, and they will try to go to the markets before the elections," said Santander Investment economist Hector Chavez.
Voters may ease the tight hold the long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) has on the lower house of Congress, and change the governors in several states on July 6.
One of the most eagerly awaited votes will be in Mexico City where people will vote for a governor for the first time. The PRI's hold on the Senate is not in question.

Mexico already went to capital markets early this year, placing a $1.0 billion 10-year global bond at the start of January, and used those funds to help back the U.S. Treasury and the International Monetary Fund.

The UMS has $1.4 billion in maturing debt this year, but various state agencies, such as federal Electricty Commission and state oil monopoly Pemex, also have issues coming due this year, bringing the market total to $4.047 billion.
Mexican corporate issuers could also be pushed by the upcoming elections to go to the market early, said analysts.

"You hear Mexican companies saying that if you are going to do it you should do it by March, before the elections or they will have to wait until September, in order to avoid political turbulence," said Ing Barings' Head of Latin American Corporate Debt Research, Anne Milne.

While the federal government could go to capital markets early to meet its needs for the debt it has maturing, analysts say the government is also considering buying back more outstanding Brady bonds.
One possible avenue would be for Mexico to exercise its option to call its Aztec Brady bonds at the end of March, Santander said recently.

By calling the Aztecs, Mexico releases the U.S. Treasury zero coupon collateral, which represents almost half the value of the Aztecs, so the issue could be refinanced with a new issuance of only half the size, reducing Mexico's debt by over $1.0 billion (U.S.), Santander's Julian Eisner said in a report.
In September, Mexico issued a $1.0 billion 20-year global bond aimed at buying back outstanding Discount Brady bonds.
The value recovery rights tied to the price of oil on the outstanding Mexican Par and Discount Brady bonds are also becoming more valuable as oil prices remain strong.
The December 1996 VRR payments were officially published at $216.93 per million face of Mexican Par bonds and, by implication, $333.74 per million discount bonds, Bear Stearns said recently.
But with benchmark oil prices reaching the highest levels in years, "we expect that the March 1997 payment will exceed our earlier calculations," Bear Stearns said.
Bear Stearns sovereign debt analyst Tulio Vera said that he did not expect the higher value recovery rights alone would be enough to tip Mexico into another Brady buyback.
((-- Mexico City newsroom (525) 728 9559))
